questions.question_text: Which of the following antipsychotics is the fastest to dissociate from the dopamine D2 receptor?
questions.explanation: Clozapine is an antagonist of 5-HT2A, D1, D3, and D4. It also has potent antagonism of muscarinic M1, H1, and α1-adrenergic receptors. It has relatively low potency as a D2 receptor antagonist. At therapeutic doses, clozapine occupies fewer D2 receptors than the other antipsychotics, and its looser (‘fast’) dissociation from the D2 receptor may allow more normal dopamine neurotransmission and a lower risk of extrapyramidal side effects.

questions.question_text: Which of the following street drugs has local anaesthetic properties?
questions.explanation: Cocaine has membrane-stabilising effects and thus local anaesthetic properties. Historically, Freud used cocaine for its local anaesthetic action during treatment of his tongue cancer.

questions.question_text: A 41-year-old woman taking disulfiram to aid abstinence from alcohol presents with flushing, hypotension and tachycardia. She denies alcohol intake. Which of the following might explain her symptoms?
questions.explanation: Many over-the-counter cough and cold preparations contain enough ethanol to precipitate a disulfiram–alcohol reaction. When disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, acetaldehyde accumulates and causes flushing, nausea, vomiting, hypotension and tachycardia.

questions.question_text: The antiemetic property of chlorpromazine is mainly due to:
questions.explanation: Chlorpromazine’s antiemetic action is principally through D2-receptor blockade in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, which suppresses nausea and vomiting.

questions.question_text: Sally is taking amisulpride and complains of amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and loss of sexual desire. This effect is caused by:
questions.explanation: Antagonism of D2 receptors in the tuberoinfundibular pathway disinhibits prolactin release, resulting in hyperprolactinaemia. Elevated prolactin causes galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea and decreased libido.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a known psychiatric effect of the drug clonidine?
questions.explanation: The main adverse effects of clonidine are sedation, postural hypotension, and depression.

questions.question_text: The term "intrinsic activity" of a drug-receptor complex refers to:

options.text: The efficiency of a drug in reaching the appropriate receptors
Potency of the drug to cause a functional response
Affinity of the drug to the receptor
Efficacy of the resulting functional response
The receptor action in the absence of the drug molecule

correct_answer.text: Efficacy of the resulting functional response

correct_answers.text: Efficacy of the resulting functional response

questions.explanation: Intrinsic activity refers to the capability of a drug-receptor complex to produce the highest functional response (i.e. efficacy).

questions.question_text: Gamma hydroxybutyrate (GHB) acts on which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation: Sodium oxybate is also known as gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), and acts as a full agonist at GHB receptors and a partial agonist at GABA-B  receptors. GHB is a natural product in the brain and formed by the neurotransmitter GABA. It has been labeled a ‘date rape’ drug as it can  be used with alcohol for this purpose, knocking someone out and causing amnesia for the time while involuntarily intoxicated. Because it  profoundly increases slow-wave sleep and the growth hormone surge that accompanies slow wave sleep, it was also used (abused) by  athletes as a performance-enhancing drug, especially in the 1980s when it was sold over the counter in health food stores. GHB is used in  some European countries as a treatment for alcoholism.

questions.question_text: A patient on cyclosporine presents with depression. Which antidepressant must be avoided as first-line because it inhibits CYP3A4 and raises cyclosporine levels?
questions.explanation: Fluoxetine (as well as fluvoxamine and nefazodone) is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor and can significantly increase cyclosporine levels.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old on lithium develops systemic hypertension. Which antihypertensive is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors (e.g. captopril) can reduce thirst (which can lead to mild dehydration) and increase renal sodium loss (leading to increased  sodium re-absorption by the kidney), resulting in an increase in lithium plasma levels. The magnitude of this e ect is variable, from no  increase to a four-fold increase. Diuretics can reduce the renal clearance of lithium, the magnitude of this e ect being greater with thiazide  than loop diuretics. Lithium levels usually rise within 10 days of a thiazide diuretic (e.g. bendroumethiazide, chlortalidone, inadapamide,  xipamide) being prescribed. Although there are case reports of lithium toxicity induced by loop diuretics, many patients receive loop  diuretics (e.g. furosemide) together with lithium without apparent problems.

questions.question_text: The safest diuretic to use with lithium is:
questions.explanation: The following are loop diuretics- furosemide, bumetanide and torasemide. Although there are case reports of lithium toxicity induced by  loop diuretics, many patients receive this combination of drugs without apparent problems. Patients taking blood diuretics may also have  been advised to restrict their salt intake, which may contribute to the risk of lithium toxicity in these individuals. With the use of Thiazide  diuretics (bendroumethiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide, metolazone, xipamide), care is required, as these classes of drugs can reduce  the renal clearance of lithium and precipitate toxicity. (Ref: The Maudsley prescribing guidelines)

questions.question_text: A patient on MAOI can safely consume:
questions.explanation: The most worrisome side e ect of MAOIs is the tyramine-induced hypertensive crisis (‘cheese reaction’). The amino acid tyramine is normally  transformed via GI metabolism. However, MAOIs inactivate GI metabolism of dietary tyramine, thus allowing intact tyramine to enter the  circulation. A hypertensive crisis may subsequently occur because of a powerful pressor e ect of the amino acid. Sources of dietary  tyramine include cheese, meat extracts and yeast extracts, alcohol, non-fresh sh, non-fresh poultry, o al, avocado, banana skins, broad  bean pods, caviar, and herring (pickled or smoked). Unlike the others listed, grapefruit juice is not rich in tyramine.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding diazepam?

options.text: Has an inactive metabolite called desmethyldiazepam
Presence of food increases extent of absorption

questions.explanation: Diazepam has an elimination half-life of 20-50 hours. The fact that all benzodiazepines are lipid-soluble to varying degrees means that  benzodiazepines and their active metabolites bind to plasma proteins. The extent of this binding is proportional to their lipid solubility. The  amount of protein binding varies from 70-99% (approximately 95% for diazepam). Diazepam is oxidised to desmethyldiazepam, which, in  turn, is hydroxylated to produce oxazepam. These products undergo glucuronidation to inactive metabolites. Food does not a ect  absorption

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is true of mianserin?

options.text: Inhibits uptake of both noradrenaline and 5-HT
Has a plasma half-life that allows once-daily dosage

correct_answer.text: Has a plasma half-life that allows once-daily dosage

correct_answers.text: Has a plasma half-life that allows once-daily dosage

questions.explanation: Mianserin is a potent inhibitor of Noradrenaline uptake with little e ect on 5-HT. It is an alpha 2 antagonist and has weak alpha 1  antagonism. It is mildly sedative and has weak antimuscarinic e ects. It is rapidly absorbed from the gut with the peak plasma concentration  appearing in less than 3 hours after a single oral dose. The plasma half-life is 10-29 hours.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a phase II metabolic reaction?
questions.explanation: Conjugation, N-acetylation, methylation and glucuronidation are phase 2 reactions. Oxidation and hydrolysis are phase 1 reactions.

questions.question_text: Which antidepressant’s plasma level correlates most strongly with therapeutic response?
questions.explanation: Clinical outcome with imipramine is clearly related to plasma levels: levels below 180 ng/ml have low probability of recovery, whereas levels above 180 ng/ml are associated with good response.

questions.question_text: Which of the following truly reflects the effects of smoking?

options.text: No tolerance develops to physical effects
Reduces risk of depression in adults

questions.explanation: Tobacco smoke contains polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons that induce (increase the activity of) certain hepatic enzymes (CYP1A2 in  particular). The extent of enzyme induction is determined by the number and type of cigarettes smoked and the degree of smoke inhalation.  For some drugs used in psychiatry, smoking signi cantly reduces drug plasma levels and higher doses are required than in non-smokers.  Smoking reduces plasma clozapine levels by up to 50%. Cigarette smoke increases ca eine metabolism and smokers may require higher  doses of ca eine to gain desired e ects.

questions.question_text: A 24-year-old man says 'My nurse needlebottoms me weeks'. He is exhibiting
questions.explanation: Paragrammatism refers to constructing sentences where words are jumbled giving rise to grammatically incorrect, but still meaningful  sentences. It is the misuse of grammar not attributable to an overall reduction of grammatical morphemes or simpli cation of syntactic  structure. Paragrammatic patients have prodigious output, leading to ‘confused sentence monsters’. Examples are: ‘And I want everything to  be so talk.’ ‘She was handled to look at the books a bit.’

questions.question_text: A patient repeatedly says “Newcastle upon Tyne” on every MMSE item after the first. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Perseveration is the inappropriate, unintentional repetition of a verbal response beyond its relevant context.

questions.question_text: A psychotic patient refers to his stomach as a “food vessel.” What speech disturbance is this?
questions.explanation: Paraphasia are normal words used unconventionally or distortedly but still recognizable in derivation.

questions.question_text: An elderly woman believes neighbors pass through walls to enter her flat. This is known as:
questions.explanation: Partition delusions have been de ned as ‘the belief that people, animals, materials, or radiation can pass through a structure that would  normally constitute a barrier to such passage. They arise as a secondary phenomenon to the primary delusional experience of being  observed, spoken about, or physically a ected by some agent outside the home.’ This type of delusion seems to be particularly common in  older adults who develop psychosis.

questions.question_text: The most common type of delusion in delusional misidentification syndromes is:
questions.explanation: Delusional misidenti cation is a delusional belief that certain individuals are not who they externally appear to be. These syndromes usually  manifest as symptoms of an underlying disorder (e.g. schizophrenia, mood disorder, delusional disorder, organic disorder) and rarely occur  in isolation. They commonly involve an element of persecution, though not always. Types of delusional misidenti cation syndromes include  Capgras, Fregoli, Intermetamorphosis, Subjective doubles, Autoscopic, Reverse subjective double, and Reverse Fregoli.

questions.question_text: A man sees repeated pleasurable images of a stranger and wonders why. This is best termed:
questions.explanation: Preoccupation denotes pleasurable or unwanted repetitive thoughts or images not characteristic of obsessions or flashbacks.

questions.question_text: He believes his wife unfaithful because he saw a blue car. This is a:
questions.explanation: Primary delusion (delusional perception) arises directly from a normal perception (blue car) interpreted in a delusional way.

questions.question_text: Prolonged sensory deprivation causes:
questions.explanation: Extended absence of normal sensory input leads to perceptual distortions and dysphoria, not euphoria.

questions.question_text: Repeated grandiose lies that a patient seems to believe are called:
questions.explanation: Pseudologia fantastica involves elaborate, self-aggrandizing untrue stories believed by the teller, distinct from delusion or deliberate lying.

questions.question_text: A man recalls a childhood event, then adds scenes until he has a complete but unverified memory. This is called:
questions.explanation: Recollection is the reintegration of a complete event from various components, reconstructing distant memories.

questions.question_text: The fundamental psychopathology in Capgras delusion is:
questions.explanation: Capgras syndrome may be a form of reduplicative paramnesia, where a person believes a familiar person has been replaced by an impostor.

questions.question_text: In mania with grandiose delusions, which type of delusion is most common?
questions.explanation: Grandiose delusions in mania are typically secondary, arising from the elevated mood state.

questions.question_text: A very religious woman believes she has a Divine Gift equal to Mother Teresa during elated periods. This is:
questions.explanation: Grandiose religious delusions in the context of euphoric mood are secondary delusions arising from the affective state.

questions.question_text: 'I have tingling feelings in my hands caused by magnetic currents from an alternator'. Identify the psychopathological terms used to describe the following experience
questions.explanation: Somatic passivity is a first rank symptom. It consists of either somatic hallucinations or normal perceptions associated with the belief that an outside agent is responsible. Delusions of control are a group of delusions which are also known as passivity phenomenon or delusions of body passivity. They are considered first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia. The core feature is the delusional belief that one is no longer in sole control of one’s own body. The individual delusions are that one is being forced by some external to feel emotions (passivity of affect or ‘made affect’), to desire to do things (passivity of impulse or ‘made impulse’), to perform actions (passivity of volition or ‘made act’), or to experience bodily sensations (somatic passivity).

questions.question_text: Which defence mechanism is a neurotic one?
questions.explanation: Neurotic defences include intellectualisation, repression, displacement, reaction formation and dissociation.

questions.question_text: Which defence mechanism is related to paranoia?
questions.explanation: Projection—attributing one's own unacceptable impulses to others—is linked to paranoid defences and persecutory delusions.

questions.question_text: A man with unconscious hate says “He hates me.” This defence is:
questions.explanation: Projection transforms an unacceptable impulse ('I hate him') into 'He hates me.'

questions.question_text: The span of immediate memory is roughly:
questions.explanation: George Miller’s work established the 'magical number seven'±2 as the capacity of immediate (working) memory.

questions.question_text: Which theory is associated with retrieval-failure forgetting?
questions.explanation: All listed theories (state/context dependence, blocking, prospective memory failure) involve retrieval failure, not encoding failure.

questions.question_text: Abnormal performance on the Stroop test suggests:
questions.explanation: The Stroop effect measures inhibitory control and attentional bias; impairment is linked to frontal lobe lesions.

questions.question_text: Tom is conditioned to fear a rabbit after pairing it with a loud noise. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Classical conditioning occurs when a neutral stimulus (rabbit) is paired with an unconditioned stimulus (loud noise) to elicit a conditioned response (fear).

questions.question_text: The process that transfers information from short-term to long-term memory is called:
questions.explanation: Memory consolidation stabilises and integrates new information into long-term storage.

questions.question_text: All of the following are tests of recent memory EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Digit span assesses working (immediate) memory, not anterograde (recent) memory.

questions.question_text: A phobic patient improves with repeated crowd exposure. Which learning process is this?
questions.explanation: Extinction occurs when a conditioned response decreases after the conditioned stimulus (crowds) is presented without the aversive outcome.

questions.question_text: If a parent ignores a child’s misbehaviour (withholding attention), this is an example of:
questions.explanation: Withdrawing attention (the positive reinforcer) leads to extinction of the unwanted behaviour.

questions.question_text: Which theory proposed that emotion is secondary to physiological changes with distinct patterns for each emotion?
questions.explanation: James–Lange theory states that physiological changes precede and give rise to subjective emotional experience.

questions.question_text: Whose theory held that thinking occurs peripherally in the speech apparatus?
questions.explanation: John Watson’s peripheralism proposed that thinking is subvocal speech—activity in the peripheral speech apparatus.

questions.question_text: Whose theory of emotions proposed that emotion is secondary to physiological changes and that there is a distinct pattern of changes for different emotions?
questions.explanation: James–Lange theory holds that physiological changes occur first and that distinct patterns of these changes give rise to specific emotions.

questions.question_text: Who postulated that thinking occurs peripherally in the speech apparatus?
questions.explanation: John Watson’s peripheralism proposed that thought is subvocal speech—activity in the speech apparatus rather than central cognitive processing.

questions.question_text: Which of the following are correctly paired with the concepts they introduced?
questions.explanation: Carl Jung developed the personality typology distinguishing introversion and extraversion.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is not one of the Gestalt principles of perception?
questions.explanation: Gestalt laws include proximity, similarity, closure, continuity and common fate. Familiarity is not one of the classic Gestalt principles.

questions.question_text: Beautiful people are generally viewed as more kind, convincing and effective. This is called:
questions.explanation: The halo effect is our tendency to let one salient trait (e.g. attractiveness) influence our judgement of other characteristics.

questions.question_text: Which of the following ethical principles does the issue of capacity to make treatment decisions uphold?
questions.explanation: Autonomy is the principle that individuals have the right to make informed decisions about their own care when they have capacity.

questions.question_text: Under the principle of necessity which of the following can be done without the patient’s consent?

options.text: Covert medication in a competent non‐consenting adult
Detention of a voluntary psychiatric inpatient who is attempting to leave
Sterilisation of a patient with postpartum mania
Blood sample to confirm MI in an unconscious schizophrenia patient

correct_answer.text: Blood sample to confirm MI in an unconscious schizophrenia patient

correct_answers.text: Blood sample to confirm MI in an unconscious schizophrenia patient

questions.explanation: Emergency, potentially life‐saving interventions (e.g. drawing blood to diagnose MI in an unconscious patient) may be performed under necessity.

questions.question_text: The Tarasoff case is related to which ethical principle?
questions.explanation: The Tarasoff ruling established a duty to warn/protect third parties over the duty of patient confidentiality when there is a credible threat.

questions.question_text: According to the Holmes and Rahe Social Readjustment Scale, which event has the highest life‐change value?
questions.explanation: Death of a spouse is assigned 100 life‐change units—the highest score on the Holmes‐Rahe Stress Scale.

questions.question_text: Which of the following ethical theories concerns itself with the intent behind actions rather than consequences?
questions.explanation: Deontology (Kantian ethics) focuses on moral duties and the intentions behind actions rather than their outcomes.

questions.question_text: A patient demands a CT scan for migraine. Your judgment says it’s unnecessary. The best option is:

options.text: Refuse and tell the patient to find another doctor
Refuse and discharge from your care
Order the CT to avoid complaints
Decline and offer a second‐opinion referral

correct_answer.text: Decline and offer a second‐opinion referral

correct_answers.text: Decline and offer a second‐opinion referral

questions.explanation: If a request is clinically unwarranted, you should explain your reasoning and offer a second‐opinion referral rather than acquiesce or abandon the patient.

questions.question_text: In some families, contradictory parental demands on children lead to confusion and frustration. This is called:
questions.explanation: A double‐bind involves two conflicting messages, creating no satisfactory response and leading to confusion.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for ADHD?
questions.explanation: Well‐conducted studies have not confirmed food additives or sugar as causes of ADHD.

questions.question_text: All of the following commonly influence health explanatory models EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Cultural background, age, gender, education and the point in time/context can shape explanatory models; past good health does not.

questions.question_text: At what age does ‘theory of mind’ fully develop?
questions.explanation: By around 4 years old, children understand that others can hold false beliefs—key to a mature theory of mind.

questions.question_text: Which infants do not attempt to interact with the mother nor seem upset when left with a stranger?
questions.explanation: Anxious/avoidant infants show little protest at separation and avoid interaction on reunion.

questions.question_text: Which experiment is NOT correctly matched with Piaget’s stages?
questions.explanation: Conservation tasks are mastered in the concrete operational stage, not the sensorimotor stage.

questions.question_text: A 4‐year‐old hides an object on his head, believing others can’t see it. In Piaget’s terms this is:
questions.explanation: Egocentrism at the pre‐operational stage means the child assumes others share his viewpoint.

questions.question_text: Which fear is present at birth?
questions.explanation: Newborns reflexively startle or show distress at sudden loud noises.

questions.question_text: Family instability affects children differently. Which is correct?

options.text: Hyperactive children more affected than easy‐going
Younger children less affected than older

correct_answer.text: Hyperactive children more affected than easy‐going

correct_answers.text: Hyperactive children more affected than easy‐going

questions.explanation: Hyperactive, young children in larger families and lower SES are more vulnerable to behavioural and cognitive difficulties.

questions.question_text: Which is NOT an effect of parental divorce?
questions.explanation: Children of divorce often show emotional and behavioural problems; increased academic motivation is not a typical effect.

questions.question_text: According to Erikson, between ages 6 and 11 the crisis to be resolved is:
questions.explanation: In the industry vs inferiority stage, children develop a sense of competence through learning and peer interaction.

questions.question_text: Which programme is appropriate for children and adults with communication and learning difficulties?
questions.explanation: Makaton is a sign and symbol language system designed specifically to support people with communication and learning difficulties.

questions.question_text: Which drug can cause whitish‐brown granular deposits in the cornea and lens?
questions.explanation: High‐dose chlorpromazine can produce corneal and lens pigmentation, which resolves on drug withdrawal.

questions.question_text: Risk factors for tardive dyskinesia include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Tardive dyskinesia is linked to chronic antipsychotic use and factors like age, comorbidities and anticholinergics, not short‐term treatment.

questions.question_text: Rabbit syndrome (mouth tremors) results from blockade of which receptor?
questions.explanation: Rabbit syndrome is a lip and perioral tremor due to D2‐receptor blockade and is a form of extrapyramidal symptom.

questions.question_text: A patient on 600 mg/day clozapine has a seizure. The most appropriate next step is:
questions.explanation: After a clozapine‐related seizure, hold one day and restart at a lower dose, with or without an anticonvulsant like valproate if indicated.

questions.question_text: Benzodiazepine withdrawal is associated with:
questions.explanation: Tolerance to benzodiazepines may involve down‐regulation of GABA–benzodiazepine receptors, leading to decreased GABA function on withdrawal.

questions.question_text: A 48‐year‐old man on olanzapine with BMI 38, drowsiness and erectile dysfunction most likely has:
questions.explanation: Olanzapine is associated with weight gain, sedation and metabolic syndrome, including insulin resistance and diabetes.

questions.question_text: Which drug can markedly increase blood acetaldehyde concentration?
questions.explanation: Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing acetaldehyde accumulation and severe reactions if alcohol is consumed.

questions.question_text: A 33‐year‐old woman on fluoxetine wishes to conceive. If she continues fluoxetine, her risk of major malformations is:
questions.explanation: SSRIs are associated with a small increase in the risk of major congenital malformations, primarily cardiac.

questions.question_text: The drug of choice for restless legs syndrome is:
questions.explanation: Dopamine agonists such as pramipexole or ropinirole are first‐line treatments for restless legs syndrome.

questions.question_text: In patients receiving lithium therapy, which can be observed even at normal therapeutic doses?
questions.explanation: Therapeutic lithium may cause benign ECG changes such as T-wave flattening or inversion without clinical consequences.

questions.question_text: One among the following is NOT a feature of serotonin syndrome:
questions.explanation: Shock‐like sensations are characteristic of SSRI discontinuation syndrome, not serotonin syndrome.

questions.question_text: Which serious adverse effect is associated with tacrine?
questions.explanation: Tacrine, an early cholinesterase inhibitor for dementia, carries a risk of hepatotoxicity requiring liver‐function monitoring.

questions.question_text: Which is a predisposing factor for QT prolongation?
questions.explanation: Women have longer baseline QT intervals and are at higher risk for drug‐induced QT prolongation.

questions.question_text: Thromboembolism as a side effect of clozapine is most likely to occur in:
questions.explanation: Clozapine‐associated thromboembolism most often occurs within the first six months of treatment.

questions.question_text: Which statement is true about neural correlates of sign language in deaf patients?

options.text: Occipital lobe takes over language processing
No involvement of normal language areas
Left temporal lesions impair sign comprehension
Aphasias not seen in sign language users

correct_answer.text: Left temporal lesions impair sign comprehension

correct_answers.text: Left temporal lesions impair sign comprehension

questions.explanation: Comprehension of sign language activates left temporal language areas; lesions here can cause sign‐language comprehension deficits.

questions.question_text: Damage unilaterally to which region produces an upper quadrantanopia?
questions.explanation: The lower bank of the calcarine fissure represents the upper visual field; lesions there cause upper quadrant field loss.

questions.question_text: The best test to measure premorbid IQ in a patient with apparent decline is:
questions.explanation: The NART estimates premorbid IQ in English speakers by testing pronunciation of irregular words.

questions.question_text: Broca’s aphasia is also known as:
questions.explanation: Broca’s aphasia features non‐fluent, effortful speech with relatively intact comprehension.

questions.question_text: Which cognitive test is useful to assess semantic memory?
questions.explanation: Semantic memory for word meaning and general knowledge is tested by object naming and defining word meanings.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is a neuropsychological theory of ADHD?
questions.explanation: ADHD is associated with impairments in executive functions mediated by fronto‐striatal circuits.

questions.question_text: Lesion of which lobe causes nominal aphasia (anomia)?
questions.explanation: Anomic aphasia is most consistently linked to lesions in the left parietal lobe, especially the angular gyrus.

questions.question_text: Jane experiences sensory aura with tingling, numbness with vague pain sensations, body image distortions, vertigo and visual illusions. The most likely seat of epileptic focus is
questions.explanation: Parietal lobe seizures often produce positive or negative sensory phenomena and body‐image distortions.

questions.question_text: Which is a performance subscale of the WAIS?
questions.explanation: WAIS performance subtests include picture completion, block design, digit‐symbol, picture arrangement and object assembly.

questions.question_text: Lesion of which structure causes bitemporal hemianopia?
questions.explanation: A pituitary tumor compressing the optic chiasm produces loss of the temporal visual fields in both eyes.

questions.question_text: Alexia without agraphia (pure alexia) is seen in lesions of:
questions.explanation: Pure alexia arises from infarction in the left posterior cerebral artery territory, affecting the visual cortex and splenium.

questions.question_text: A major use of the Glasgow Coma Scale is to:
questions.explanation: The GCS is widely used in acute brain injury to stratify severity and predict mortality.

questions.question_text: A 43-year-old man can speak normally and comprehend what is spoken. He can also write spontaneously and to dictation, but reading comprehension is impaired.
questions.explanation: Pure word blindness (alexia without agraphia) involves preserved writing and speech but impaired reading comprehension.

questions.question_text: Immediate repetition of 3 items in MMSE is used to test
questions.explanation:
Immediate repetition of 3 items in MMSE is used to test 'Registration'.
Delayed recall can be tested by asking to repeat the items after a distraction test

questions.question_text: Which of the following components of transcribed RNA is removed before translation occurs?
questions.explanation: An intron is any nucleotide sequence within a gene that is removed before generating the final mature RNA product of a gene. Introns are removed by a process called splicing before protein translation begins. The ribonucleoprotein assembly that removes the intervening sequences from pre-mRNAs through splicing is called the spliceosome.

questions.question_text: Which of the following genetic element is implicated in Huntington's disease?
questions.explanation: The mutation in the IT-15 gene ('interesting transcript 15') on chromosome 4 with an unstable region of the harbouring an expanded trinucleotide repeat motif, is associated with Huntington's disease.

questions.question_text: The term used for the purpose of identifying the locus of a gene on the chromosome by studying the extent to which it co-segregates with a marker gene is called
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
Linkage analysis is used to obtain a coarse chromosomal location of the genes associated with a phenotype under investigation (e.g. a genetic disease or an important quantitative trait). All genetic mapping methods aim to identify disease-associated variants based on their chromosomal position and the principle of genetic linkage. Genes that are physically close to one another on a chromosome are genetically linked, and those that are further apart or are on different chromosomes are genetically unlinked. Unlinked genes will recombine at random. Genetic loci that are linked will recombine less frequently than expected by random segregation, with the degree of recombination proportional to the physical distance between them.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 988.

questions.question_text: Two parents are both affected with the same autosomal recessive disorder give birth to a clinically normal child. Which of the following can explain the above?
questions.explanation:
Locus heterogeneity refers to mutations at several different loci producing identical phenotypes.
A good example is presenilin1, 2 and Beta APP mutations all causing phenotypically similar presenile Alzheimer's dementia.
In this example, each parent may have had a different mutation, so the child is a heterozygote carrier at both loci.

questions.question_text: The term used to describe a point mutation that leads to failure of expression of alleles is
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
Loss-of-function mutations are the result of gene product having less or no function. Phenotypes associated with such mutations are most often recessive. Loss-of-function mutations abolish a gene’s biomolecular activity. The existence of a category of alleles distinguished by a derived loss of biochemical functions has been described by various names: amorphic, loss-of-function, non-functional, knockout, null, pseudogene, or gene loss. Total gene loss is the most obvious case of loss of function. Yet total gene loss is not the only means by which loss of function can occur. Single mutations and many mutation types such as premature stop codons, frameshifts, splice site disruptions, and elimination of regulatory regions required for gene expression can have effects that are functionally indistinguishable from complete gene loss.
Ref: Monroe JG, McKay JK, Weigel D, Flood PJ. The population genomics of adaptive loss of function. Heredity. 2021 Mar;126(3):383-95.

questions.question_text: Following a Robertsonian translocation in phenotypically normal individual which of the following types of chromosomes is produced?
questions.explanation: Following a Robertsonian translocation, the small 'p' arms are discarded, and a metacentric fusion chromosome results.

questions.question_text: A family with three affected children has a higher recurrence risk for a disease than another family with only two affected children. This disease is most likely to be inherited via
questions.explanation: An increasing recurrence risk according to the number of relatives affected is seen in multifactorial diseases. Recurrence risks for Mendelian disorders are unaffected by number of offsprings already affected.

questions.question_text: Which of the following disorders is associated with HLA-DQB1*-0602?
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
Narcolepsy is a chronic disorder that is primarily characterised by excessive daytime sleepiness and, in most individuals, cataplexy. The latest edition of the International Classification of Sleep Disorders has reclassified narcolepsy into narcolepsy type 1 (NT1) and NT2. This is based on the finding that the absence of the hypocretin peptides (also known as orexins; which are neuropeptides with a role in the regulation of sleep and wakefulness) is a fundamental marker in most patients with narcolepsy with cataplexy. Patients with NT1 have cataplexy and/or low levels of hypocretin 1 (also known as orexin A) in the CSF, whereas patients with NT2 do not have cataplexy and have normal levels of hypocretin 1. The main genetic risk for narcolepsy is the HLA-DQB1*06:02 allele, which explains the majority of the known genetic effects in NT1. Depending on the population, 86-98% of patients with NT1 carry the HLA-DQB1*06:02 allele.
Ref: Kornum BR et al. Narcolepsy. Nature reviews Disease primers. 2017 Feb 9;3(1):1-9.
